lesson.title: Freezing the Wave: The Phasor Shortcut
lesson.summary: A phasor packages a sinusoid's amplitude and phase into a single complex number, turning tedious trigonometric bookkeeping into ordinary complex-number algebra.
lesson.body:
Every sinusoidal voltage and current sharing a single frequency ω carries the same spinning factor e^(jωt) through every calculation: adding, multiplying, differentiating, over and over. A phasor removes that redundancy. Since ω is common to every signal in a linear circuit driven by one source, it can be tracked once, in the background, while the real bookkeeping happens on amplitude and phase alone. This turns differential equations in time into ordinary algebra with complex numbers, which is why phasor analysis is the backbone of essentially every AC circuit technique.

The bridge from a time-domain cosine to a phasor is Euler's formula, e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ. A sinusoid v(t) = Vm cos(ωt + φ) can be rewritten as the real part of a rotating complex exponential: v(t) = Re[Vm e^(j(ωt+φ))] = Re[(Vm e^(jφ)) e^(jωt)]. The bracketed piece, Vm e^(jφ), does not depend on time at all; it is the phasor, usually written in polar form as Vm∠φ. By convention in circuit analysis, phasors are built from rms magnitudes rather than peak amplitudes, so the phasor of v(t) is actually V = (Vm/√2)∠φ; this matches how AC meters read voltage and keeps power formulas free of stray factors of two.

Take the voltage v(t) = 170 cos(377t − 30°) V from the sinusoidal waveform discussion. Its rms magnitude is 170/√2 = 120.2 V, rounded to 120 V for a nominal household supply, and its phase angle is −30°. The phasor is therefore V = 120∠−30° V. Written in rectangular form, V = 120 cos(−30°) + j120 sin(−30°) = 120(0.8660) + j120(−0.5000) = 103.9 − j60.0 V; polar and rectangular forms represent the exact same complex number, converted using the same trigonometry as any other polar-form problem.

A phasor is not a real, physical thing frozen in space; it is a bookkeeping device, a snapshot of a spinning quantity read at one instant. To recover the original time-domain signal, multiply the phasor by e^(jωt) and take the real part again: v(t) = Re[V√2 e^(jωt)], where the √2 restores the peak amplitude from the rms phasor. This reversibility is what makes phasors trustworthy: nothing is lost in translation, only the repeated e^(jωt) factor is set aside so that addition, subtraction, and impedance calculations can be done with ordinary complex-number algebra instead of trigonometric identities. That algebraic simplicity is the entire payoff, and it is what makes phasor diagrams and phasor addition, covered next, so much easier than working directly with cosines.

Not every problem can be phasor-ized this simply: phasor algebra only works because every signal in the circuit shares the identical angular frequency ω, which is guaranteed whenever a linear circuit, resistors, inductors, capacitors, is driven by a single sinusoidal source. If two voltages of different frequencies were added, say 60 Hz and 120 Hz, their phasors could not simply be summed, because the assumption that let e^(jωt) cancel out no longer holds; each frequency component would need its own separate phasor analysis. This restriction rarely causes trouble in practice, since most AC power circuits are driven by a single frequency, but it marks the exact boundary of where the shortcut applies.
